name: Gareth Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Gareth. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to tech firms, employers or parties, and your answers stay confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the sales reporting team at the head office of a big supermarket chain, seven analysts in an open-plan room above the car park. We tell the buyers and store managers what sold, what didn't, and why the frozen pizza numbers in the north look strange this week. I spend the morning checking the reports and the afternoon in meetings explaining them to people who'd rather not hear it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love finding the story in the numbers, like when we worked out that a bad batch of oven chips was why one region looked weak. What drains me is the copying and pasting. Or it did, until last year, when I set up AI tools to build half our weekly reports for us. I use them every day now, for code, for summaries, for nearly everything.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a two-bedroom flat my grandad left me, and my friend Owen rents the spare room. So I've got no mortgage, a lodger paying some bills, and over a year of savings. Politically I'm the one at family dinners arguing for a four-day week and taxing the big tech firms properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got sold as magic. At work I'd keep showing people the boring jobs it can do, because those savings are real even if they're small. Online I'd probably post something smug about the investors who lost money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be slightly disappointed. I like this stuff, and I'd hoped it would free people from the dull parts of their jobs. For me personally, though, nothing changes, and my job's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep building small tools for the team. I'd probably put a bit more of my savings into a pension, since prices and pay would just carry on as normal. I might teach a short lunchtime session for other head office teams on the simple tricks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit flat, like a film that didn't live up to the trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You built tools that do half the reports. Did anyone lose work because of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We used the time to do deeper work, like the oven chips story. But I won't pretend that would always be true. If my boss Hannah had needed to cut costs, those saved hours would have been the first thing she looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would bother you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me. The thing I'd watch is the stores, because the self-checkouts already cut shifts without any clever AI. Owen works at one of our stores on the tills, and he's lost four hours a week since the spring.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** that got sold as magic.
I'd keep showing colleagues the **boring jobs** it can do, because those savings are real.
think: I'd be slightly **disappointed**, because I hoped it would free people from dull work.
My own **job is safe**, and nothing really changes for me.
do: Keep building **small tools** for the reporting team.
Put a bit more of my savings into a **pension**.
Teach a **lunchtime session** for other head office teams.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit flat, like a film that missed its trailer.
S0.quote: If my boss Hannah had needed to cut costs, those saved hours would have been the first thing she looked at.
fieldNote: He is secure: **no mortgage**, a lodger and over a year saved.
He's honest that **saved hours** could have become cuts under a different boss.
He notices job losses from **self-checkouts** affecting his lodger, not from AI.

steps.text: Keep building small AI tools for the weekly reports
Pay more of his savings into his pension
Teach a lunchtime session on AI tricks for head office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when the gains need sharing, through shorter hours rather than fewer people. At work I'd argue that we cut the week before we cut the team. Online I'd back the four-day week campaign, and I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do quite well out of this, and that's uncomfortable. I'm the person head office would ask to set up the new tools. My job probably grows, while two or three of my analysts' jobs shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the rollout, partly so I can shape it and protect people. I'd train every analyst on the tools so nobody is the person who can't use them. And I'd join the managers' branch of the union, which I've avoided because it felt a bit grand for a 27-year-old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, bad for people I like, and I'm the one holding the screwdriver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel being the one who automates your colleagues' work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guilty, honestly. Sam on my team is brilliant at checking the numbers by hand, and checking is on that card. I'd rather train Sam to build the tools than watch the tools replace Sam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets the gains, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, the shareholders. That's my whole argument. If the company saves the cost of three analysts, at least some of that should go into training and shorter hours, not straight to the dividend.

say: I'd say the gains must be shared through **shorter hours**, not fewer people.
I'd back the **four-day week** campaign, loudly.
think: I'd **do quite well**, as the person head office asks to run the tools.
My job grows while two or three **analysts' jobs** shrink, and that's uncomfortable.
do: Volunteer to **lead the rollout** so I can shape it and protect people.
Train every analyst on the **AI tools**.
Join the **managers' union** branch I've avoided until now.
feel: **Uneasy**: good for me, bad for people I like.
S1.quote: Good for me, bad for people I like, and I'm the one holding the screwdriver.
fieldNote: He expects his own role to **grow**, which leaves him uneasy rather than worried.
His guilt about **automating colleagues** shapes his push for shorter hours.
He wants gains shared, not sent **to shareholders**, in line with his politics.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the AI rollout in the reporting team
Train all seven analysts on the new tools
Join the managers' branch of the union
Campaign publicly for a four-day week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a national dividend, a share of what AI makes paid to everyone. I'd say it at work, at dinner, and online, and I'd help organise for it. A shorter week won't be enough if the work itself disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job goes by 2028, maybe 2029. Reporting is pure thinking work. I'd be useful for a year setting it up, then I'd be the person who switched off his own team and himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop thinking of my salary as safe and save as much of it as I can. I'd make the spare room a proper let with a contract, since the rent becomes real income. I'd look hard at store and warehouse operations, because people still move the stock by hand until the robots come around 2031, though the planning side goes in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake to it. I'd feel like I can see the wave, and I've got a board, but it's a very big wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Doesn't that put you ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe. Being good with the tools gets you the job of installing them. After that, AGI doesn't need someone who's good with AI. It is the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Owen in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen's on the tills, so he's hands-on, and he gets the extra 3 years. But the tills were already going. I'd tell him to use those years to train for something where people want a person, like nursing or the trades.

say: I'd call for a **national dividend**, a share of AI's earnings paid to everyone.
I'd say a shorter week **won't be enough** if the work disappears.
think: My **job goes by 2028** or 2029, because reporting is pure thinking work.
I'd be useful for **a year**, then I'd switch off my team and myself.
do: Save as much **salary** as possible from now.
Make the spare room a **proper let** with a contract.
Look hard at **store operations**, where hands-on work lasts until robots arrive.
feel: **Anxious** but awake, like seeing a big wave with a board in hand.
S2.quote: Being good with the tools gets you the job of installing them.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** but has a flat, a lodger and savings for control.
He sees that **AI skills** only buy him a year once AGI arrives.
He grasps that store work gets **3 more years**, but planning roles do not.

steps.text: Save as much of his salary as possible each month
Give the lodger a formal tenancy contract for steady rent
Apply for store and warehouse operations roles
Help organise a campaign for a national AI dividend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years to set up a share for everyone before it lands. I'd write to my MP and join a group pushing for it. At work I'd say every team should have a transition plan by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, 5 years means I ride it for a while. I'd run the tools, do well for three or four years, then hit the same wall around 2031. The difference is that I'd hit it at 32 with a lot more money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead every AI project going, because it's good pay and good experience. I'd put a set amount each month into a broad index fund and keep a year of cash separate. By 2029 I'd want a plan B, maybe moving into the public sector to help design how councils use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy, productive way. Like the week before a big move, with lists everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half into a plain fund that tracks the whole market, half kept as cash. I don't want clever bets. If AI is making the big firms rich, owning a tiny slice of all of them is the least I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would worry, because she remembers the factory closures in her town. I'd tell her I've got the flat, I've got savings, and I've seen it coming. Dad would just ask whether I'm still voting for the people who want to tax it.

say: I'd say use the years to set up a **share for everyone** before AGI lands.
I'd write to my **MP** and ask for team transition plans at work.
think: I'd **ride it** for three or four years before hitting the same wall.
I'd hit that wall at **32**, with far more saved.

Put a set sum monthly into an **index fund** and keep a year of cash.
Prepare a **plan B** in public sector AI design by 2029.
feel: **Anxious** in a busy way, like the week before a big move.
S3.quote: If AI is making the big firms rich, owning a tiny slice of all of them is the least I can do.
fieldNote: He expects his role to end around **2031**, but with control over the timing.
His progressive views sit alongside a **practical** move into index funds.
He plans a move to the **public sector** to shape how councils use AI.

steps.text: Lead every AI project at head office for the next three years
Pay a fixed amount each month into a broad index fund
Apply for public sector roles designing council AI use by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and we should use it to rebuild how work and pay fit together. I'd keep campaigning for a shorter week and a dividend. I'd be one of the hopeful ones, but not quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd do very well for most of that decade. The thinking jobs shrink slowly, and I'm the person who makes the shrinking happen. By 2036 I'd be 37, with no mortgage and a lot saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep leading the tools. Around 2030 I'd start a part-time master's in public policy, so I can work on the rules rather than the reports. I'd keep investing every month and stay out of debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about other people. For myself, I'd feel I have room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Public policy, probably focused on work and welfare. Someone has to design how people get paid when the machines do the work. I'd rather be in that room than in the room switching off my own team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any risk you're being too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. A decade looks long, but my job is so close to the tools that it could shrink before AGI arrives. If my boss Hannah said my team was being halved in 2030, I'd want the master's already started.

I'd keep campaigning for a **shorter week** and a dividend.
think: I'd **do very well** for most of the decade, leading the tools.

fieldNote: The long warning leaves him secure in his own eyes, so he's **uneasy** rather than anxious.
He plans to move from **reports to rules** through a policy master's.
He hedges against his **team being halved** before AGI arrives.

steps.text: Keep leading AI tools in the reporting team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd survive it, but a lot of people around me wouldn't, and I'd be the one who helped switch things off. What would help is a guaranteed share of what AI earns, paid to everyone, plus a shorter week so the remaining work gets spread out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how strange it is to be good at the thing that ends your job. I spent a year making the tools better. Every hour I saved my team was an hour that someone upstairs could decide we didn't need.

headlineQuote: Every hour I saved my team was an hour that someone upstairs could decide we didn't need.
portrait: Gareth is a 27-year-old **reporting manager** at a supermarket head office who uses AI daily.
He owns his flat **without a mortgage**, has a lodger, and holds over a year of savings.
He is calm in AI Plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, where he'd **lead the rollout**.
He expects to **lose his job** in the AGI pictures but feels he has room to act.
His politics push for a **national dividend** and shorter week, while he invests privately.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **people around him** would be hit and he'd help switch things off.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **share of AI earnings** for everyone, plus a shorter week.
